name: Neanderthals interbred with modern humans
what: People outside Africa carry about 1 to 2% Neanderthal DNA from mixing soon after leaving Africa.
why: Proved that our ancestors and Neanderthals had children; some of those genes still affect immunity and skin.

sources.cite: Richard Green et al., "A draft sequence of the Neandertal genome", Science 328 (2010)
Kay Prüfer et al., "The complete genome sequence of a Neanderthal from the Altai Mountains", Nature 505 (2014)

name: Denisovans found from a finger bone
what: A new archaic human group was identified from DNA in a finger bone from Denisova Cave; Papuans and Aboriginal Australians carry several percent of their DNA.
why: A human population known first from genes, not from fossils.

sources.cite: David Reich et al., "Genetic history of an archaic hominin group from Denisova Cave in Siberia", Nature 468 (2010)
David Reich, Who We Are and How We Got Here (2018)

name: The Mal'ta boy links Europe and the Americas
what: A 24,000-year-old boy from Lake Baikal belongs to a population that gave about a third of Native American ancestry and also part of European ancestry.
why: Showed a "ghost population" predicted by statistics before any skeleton was found.

sources.cite: Maanasa Raghavan et al., "Upper Palaeolithic Siberian genome reveals dual ancestry of Native Americans", Nature 505 (2014)

name: One founding population for the Americas
what: Ancient genomes (Anzick-1, Upward Sun River) show Native Americans descend from a population that split from East Asians and paused in Beringia before moving south about 16,000 to 14,000 years ago.
why: Settled the long fight over whether the Americas were peopled by many waves.

sources.cite: Morten Rasmussen et al., "The genome of a Late Pleistocene human from a Clovis burial site in western Montana", Nature 506 (2014)
J. Víctor Moreno-Mayar et al., "Terminal Pleistocene Alaskan genome reveals first founding population of Native Americans", Nature 553 (2018)

name: Europe's first farmers came from Anatolia and the Aegean
what: Neolithic farmers across Europe descend from Aegean-Anatolian farmers; local hunter-gatherers mostly did not adopt farming themselves.
why: Farming spread by people moving, not just ideas.

sources.cite: Iosif Lazaridis et al., "Ancient human genomes suggest three ancestral populations for present-day Europeans", Nature 513 (2014)
Iain Mathieson et al., "Genome-wide patterns of selection in 230 ancient Eurasians", Nature 528 (2015)
Zuzana Hofmanová et al., "Early farmers from across Europe directly descended from Neolithic Aegeans", PNAS 113 (2016)

name: Hunter-gatherer ancestry comes back in farming Europe
what: Over two thousand years, farming communities absorbed more and more hunter-gatherer ancestry.
why: The two groups lived side by side for centuries.

sources.cite: Mark Lipson et al., "Parallel palaeogenomic transects reveal complex genetic history of early European farmers", Nature 551 (2017)

name: Steppe ancestry floods into Europe
what: After 3000 BCE people with Yamnaya-related ancestry from the steppe spread west; Corded Ware people in Germany have about 75% of it.
why: Strong evidence that many Indo-European languages came to Europe with this migration.

sources.cite: Wolfgang Haak et al., "Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe", Nature 522 (2015)
Morten Allentoft et al., "Population genomics of Bronze Age Eurasia", Nature 522 (2015)

name: Beaker people replace 90% of Britain's ancestry
what: Within a few centuries of 2450 BCE, the people who built Stonehenge were largely replaced by newcomers with steppe ancestry.
why: One of the biggest population turnovers known in Europe.

sources.cite: Iñigo Olalde et al., "The Beaker phenomenon and the genomic transformation of northwest Europe", Nature 555 (2018)

name: Iberia: all men's lines replaced, language partly kept
what: About 40% of Iberia's ancestry and nearly 100% of its Y chromosomes were replaced by steppe-descended newcomers, yet Basque, a non-Indo-European language, survived.
why: Shows genes and language can come apart: Basques carry the steppe Y lineage but kept their language.

sources.cite: Iñigo Olalde et al., "The genomic history of the Iberian Peninsula over the past 8000 years", Science 363 (2019)

name: Steppe ancestry reaches South Asia; the Harappans had none
what: A Harappan from Rakhigarhi (about 2500 BCE) has no steppe ancestry; steppe ancestry arrives about 2000-1500 BCE, more in groups that spoke Indo-European and in Brahmins.
why: Supports Indo-Aryan languages arriving from the north after the Indus cities.

sources.cite: Vagheesh Narasimhan et al., "The formation of human populations in South and Central Asia", Science 365 (2019)
Vasant Shinde et al., "An Ancient Harappan Genome Lacks Ancestry from Steppe Pastoralists or Iranian Farmers", Cell 179 (2019)

name: Bronze Age Anatolia lacks steppe ancestry
what: Hittite-era Anatolians have little or no Yamnaya-type ancestry.
why: The Anatolian branch of Indo-European did not come with the European migration; points to the Southern Arc idea.

sources.cite: Iosif Lazaridis et al., "The genetic history of the Southern Arc: a bridge between West Asia and Europe", Science 377 (2022)
Peter de Barros Damgaard et al., "The first horse herders and the impact of early Bronze Age steppe expansions into Asia", Science 360 (2018)

name: Minoans and Mycenaeans were close kin
what: Both descended mostly from Anatolian-derived farmers; Mycenaeans add a smaller share of steppe-related ancestry.
why: The Greeks of Linear B were not a wholly new people.

sources.cite: Iosif Lazaridis et al., "Genetic origins of the Minoans and Mycenaeans", Nature 548 (2017)

name: Etruscans were genetically like their Latin neighbours
what: Etruscans had the same steppe-related ancestry as other Iron Age Italians, yet kept a non-Indo-European language; the old idea of an origin in Lydia is not supported.
why: Another case of language not following genes.

sources.cite: Cosimo Posth et al., "The origin and legacy of the Etruscans through a 2000-year archeogenomic time transect", Science Advances 7 (2021)

name: Philistines arrived from the west, then blended in
what: Early Iron Age burials at Ashkelon show a pulse of southern European-related ancestry that was diluted within two centuries.
why: Fits texts about the Sea Peoples arriving by sea.

sources.cite: Michal Feldman et al., "Ancient DNA sheds light on the genetic origins of early Iron Age Philistines", Science Advances 5 (2019)

name: Imperial Rome drew people from the East
what: Romans of the imperial era carry much more eastern Mediterranean and Near Eastern ancestry than earlier Romans.
why: The empire's capital was a city of migrants.

sources.cite: Margaret Antonio et al., "Ancient Rome: a genetic crossroads of Europe and the Mediterranean", Science 366 (2019)

name: The Xiongnu were a mixed people
what: Xiongnu-era genomes are a mix of western and eastern steppe ancestry with large differences between elites and others.
why: The first steppe empire was multi-ethnic.

sources.cite: Choongwon Jeong et al., "A dynamic 6,000-year genetic history of Eurasia's Eastern Steppe", Cell 183 (2020)
Peter de Barros Damgaard et al., "137 ancient human genomes from across the Eurasian steppes", Nature 557 (2018)

name: Anglo-Saxon migration was large
what: Early medieval people in eastern England had up to about 76% ancestry from the continent near the North Sea.
why: Not just an elite takeover: a mass migration that brought English.

sources.cite: Joscha Gretzinger et al., "The Anglo-Saxon migration and the formation of the early English gene pool", Nature 610 (2022)

name: Lombard migration was kin-based
what: Graves in Hungary and Italy show Lombard groups moved as families with mixed ancestry.
why: Barbarian migrations were whole communities, not just war bands.

sources.cite: Carlos Eduardo Amorim et al., "Understanding 6th-century barbarian social organization and migration through paleogenomics", Nature Communications 9 (2018)

name: Avar elite came from Mongolia in a generation
what: Early Avar elites in the Carpathian basin had almost pure northeast Asian ancestry, matching flight from the Rouran collapse.
why: One of the fastest long-distance migrations known.

sources.cite: Guido Alberto Gnecchi-Ruscone et al., "Ancient genomes reveal origin and rapid trans-Eurasian migration of 7th century Avar elites", Cell 185 (2022)

name: Hungarian conquerors mixed Ugric and steppe ancestry
what: Conquest-era Hungarians carry Mansi-related, Sarmatian and Hun-period steppe ancestry; their genes faded fast in the local population, their language did not.
why: An elite language shift that lasted.

sources.cite: Zoltán Maróti et al., "The genetic origin of Huns, Avars, and conquering Hungarians", Current Biology 32 (2022)

name: The Viking world was genetically mixed
what: 442 genomes show gene flow into Scandinavia from Britain and southern Europe and Vikings who were not genetically Scandinavian.
why: Being a Viking was a way of life as much as an ancestry.

sources.cite: Ashot Margaryan et al., "Population genomics of the Viking world", Nature 585 (2020)

name: The Tarim mummies were a local population
what: The oldest Tarim Basin mummies descend from an ancient local population, not from steppe migrants, though they used dairy.
why: Challenges the idea that they brought Tocharian languages.

sources.cite: Fan Zhang et al., "The genomic origins of the Bronze Age Tarim Basin mummies", Nature 599 (2021)

name: Siberian ancestry reaches Fennoscandia
what: A Siberian-related ancestry appears in the far north by about 1500 BCE and is found in Uralic speakers today.
why: A genetic trace of Uralic languages spreading west.

sources.cite: Thiseas Lamnidis et al., "Ancient Fennoscandian genomes reveal origin and spread of Siberian ancestry in Europe", Nature Communications 9 (2018)

name: Southeast Asia: farmers on top of hunter-gatherers
what: At Man Bac in Vietnam, farmers with East Asian ancestry mixed with older Hòabìnhian foragers.
why: The "two-layer" model, linked to the spread of Austroasiatic.

sources.cite: Mark Lipson et al., "Ancient genomes document multiple waves of migration in Southeast Asian prehistory", Science 361 (2018)
Hugh McColl et al., "The prehistoric peopling of Southeast Asia", Science 361 (2018)

name: The first Remote Oceanians had almost no Papuan ancestry
what: Lapita-era people from Vanuatu and Tonga had East Asian ancestry; Papuan ancestry arrived later and replaced much of it in Vanuatu.
why: Polynesians' ancestors came quickly from Taiwan and the Philippines.

sources.cite: Pontus Skoglund et al., "Genomic insights into the peopling of the Southwest Pacific", Nature 538 (2016)
Mark Lipson et al., "Population turnover in Remote Oceania shortly after initial settlement", Current Biology 28 (2018)

name: Native Americans met Polynesians around 1200
what: Genomes from eastern Polynesia carry a small share of Native American (Colombian-related) ancestry from contact around 1150-1230 CE.
why: Contact across the Pacific before Columbus, as the sweet potato suggested.

sources.cite: Alexander Ioannidis et al., "Native American gene flow into Polynesia predating Easter Island settlement", Nature 583 (2020)

name: Bantu farmers replaced foragers in the south
what: In Malawi and nearby, ancient forager DNA is almost absent today; Bantu-speaking farmers replaced and absorbed them.
why: The genetic side of the Bantu spread.

sources.cite: Pontus Skoglund et al., "Reconstructing Prehistoric African Population Structure", Cell 171 (2017)
Etienne Patin et al., "Dispersals and genetic adaptation of Bantu-speaking populations in Africa and North America", Science 356 (2017)

name: The Thule replaced the Paleo-Eskimo
what: The Paleo-Eskimo (Dorset) of the eastern Arctic left no genetic trace in today's Inuit.
why: A whole Arctic people vanished as the Thule arrived.

sources.cite: Maanasa Raghavan et al., "The genetic prehistory of the New World Arctic", Science 345 (2014)

name: The Japanese come from three ancestries
what: Jomon foragers, Yayoi farmers from the continent, and a third East Asian influx in the Kofun period.
why: The Kofun-era wave is a surprise from ancient DNA.

sources.cite: Niall Cooke et al., "Ancient genomics reveals tripartite origins of Japanese populations", Science Advances 7 (2021)

name: Two waves into the Caribbean
what: An early Archaic population was largely replaced by Ceramic Age settlers from South America, the ancestors of the Taíno.
why: Matches the Arawakan language spread.

sources.cite: Daniel Fernandes et al., "A genetic history of the pre-contact Caribbean", Nature 590 (2021)

name: A Newgrange elite married within the family
what: A man buried in the Newgrange passage tomb was the child of a first-degree incestuous union.
why: Suggests a god-king-like elite in Neolithic Ireland.

sources.cite: Lara Cassidy et al., "A dynastic elite in monumental Neolithic society", Nature 582 (2020)

name: Scythians had both eastern and western roots
what: Iron Age steppe nomads were mixed from western Yamnaya-related and eastern Asian populations.
why: Scythians formed on the steppe, not from one migration.

sources.cite: Martina Unterländer et al., "Ancestry and demography and descendants of Iron Age nomads of the Eurasian Steppe", Nature Communications 8 (2017)

name: Yellow River farmers spread south and west
what: Ancestry of Yellow River millet farmers spreads into the Tibetan plateau and southern China.
why: Consistent with the spread of Sino-Tibetan from the north.

sources.cite: Chao Ning et al., "Ancient genomes from northern China suggest links between subsistence changes and human migration", Nature Communications 11 (2020)
Chuan-Chao Wang et al., "Genomic insights into the formation of human populations in East Asia", Nature 591 (2021)
